834.title: Far-off sangats
834.hook: early sangats grew in Kabul, Dhaka and Patna, sending offerings and receiving letters
834.howItsDone: Sikhs honor Takht Sri Patna Sahib as Guru Gobind Singh's birthplace, and gurdwaras in places the Gurus visited keep the memory of the early sangats that gathered there.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a roll call of the Gurus' Muslim friends, from Mardana to Rai Kalha. Your line was friends in every faith. Did your thank-you go out? Today, friends of the Guru who lived very far from him. Day eight hundred thirty-four.

Anandpur, and a caravan coming in from the northwest, over the mountain passes, dusty and tired. Tradition says it's the sangat of Kabul, bringing gifts for the Guru, among them a fine canopy. They've traveled a very long way to stand in his presence for a little while. Then they'll turn around and make the whole journey again, home to a city where the Guru may never set foot. Today: far-off sangats.
screen: `A CARAVAN FROM KABUL.` → `GIFTS FOR THE GURU.` → `THEN THE LONG ROAD HOME.`

segments.voice: Sangat means the company, the gathered community. A listener might assume the Sikhs of the Gurus' time all lived around Punjab, within a few days' walk. Tradition tells a wider story. Guru Nanak traveled far, and where he went, people remembered. Later Gurus traveled too. Tradition says Guru Tegh Bahadur journeyed east through Patna and on to Dhaka and Assam, and sangats in those places kept his memory and their gatherings going after he left. Sikhs remember Patna, on the Ganges, as the place where Guru Gobind Singh was born and spent his early childhood, cared for by the sangat there. To the northwest, there was Kabul. So how did a sangat a long journey away stay close to a Guru it might never see? Three ways run through the stories. First, they gave. Far-off Sikhs sent offerings, a share of their earnings, carried by travelers and representatives to the Guru's court. Second, they came. Some, like the Kabul sangat in the hook, made the long trip themselves when they could. Third, they listened. Letters went out from the Guru to these sangats, read aloud when they gathered. That third thread is tomorrow's whole story, so we'll leave the letters sealed for now. What matters today is the shape of it. Distance didn't make these Sikhs second-class. In the tellings, their gatherings are sangats in full: singing the Gurus' hymns, keeping their own kitchens, and sending their love across mountains and rivers. A sangat, in this story, isn't measured by how close it sits to the center. It's measured by whether it keeps gathering.
screen: `SANGATS IN KABUL, DHAKA, PATNA.` · `THEY GAVE.` · `THEY CAME.` · `THEY LISTENED.` · then, large: `FAR OFF, STILL CLOSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of a far-off friend. Settle, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind someone who matters to you and lives far away, a long drive, a flight, a different time zone. Picture where they are right now, what time it is there, what their room might look like. Notice that the distance hasn't erased them from you. Then choose one way to close the gap a little: a gift sent, a visit planned, a long message read slowly. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Far-off sangats. The Sikh gatherings in places like Kabul, Dhaka and Patna that stayed close to the Gurus by giving, coming and listening. Today's word.
Your line: far off, still close. Today, close the gap with the far-off friend you thought of, one message or one gift. Day eight hundred thirty-four.

835.title: The Gurus' letters
835.hook: the Gurus sent signed letters to sangats, some still kept today
835.howItsDone: In gurdwaras, the Guru Granth Sahib is opened in the morning and the hymn read from the page is called the hukamnama; the daily hukamnama from the Harmandir in Amritsar is widely shared, and historic hukamnamas of the Gurus are kept with honor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the far-off sangats of Kabul, Dhaka and Patna, who gave, came and listened. Your line was far off, still close. Did you close the gap with someone far away? Today, we open the letters we left sealed. Day eight hundred thirty-five.

A bundle wrapped in cloth, in a family's keeping or a gurdwara's care. Inside, an old sheet of paper, the ink faded, the creases gone soft. At the top, tradition says, a mark linked to the Guru's own hand. Below it, lines addressed to a sangat in a faraway place, by name: a blessing, a thank-you, a request or two. Long ago it was carried in to a gathering and read aloud so that everyone could hear. Then someone folded it, and decided it would be kept. Today's word: hukamnama.
screen: `AN OLD LETTER, WRAPPED IN CLOTH.` → `ADDRESSED TO A SANGAT BY NAME.` → `READ ALOUD, THEN KEPT.`

segments.voice: A hukamnama is a letter of hukam, the Guru's command, sent to a sangat. Hukam is a big word in Sikh teaching. At the opening of the Guru Granth Sahib, in Japji, Guru Nanak teaches that everything is within the divine hukam, the order of things, and nothing stands outside it. So a hukamnama was never just mail. It carried the Guru's word to people who might never hear his voice. What did the letters say? Tradition and the surviving letters show a mix that's surprisingly human. They bless the sangat. They thank it for offerings already sent. They ask for particular things the Guru's court needed. They tell Sikhs to come when they can, to keep gathering, to live as Sikhs. Some carry the Guru's own signature or mark at the top. And some of these letters are still kept today, held by families and gurdwaras with deep honor, because a letter like that isn't something you throw out. It's a link to the Guru's own hand. Here's the part that reaches into the present. The word didn't stay in the past. Today, in gurdwaras, the Guru Granth Sahib is opened in the morning and a hymn from the open page is read out. That reading is also called the hukamnama, the day's word from the Guru. At the Harmandir in Amritsar, the day's hukamnama is shared far beyond its walls. So the far-off sangat still waits for its letter. It just arrives every morning now, from the open page.
screen: `A LETTER OF THE GURU'S HUKAM.` · `EVERYTHING IS WITHIN HUKAM.` · `SOME LETTERS ARE STILL KEPT.` · `THE DAY'S HUKAMNAMA, TODAY.` · then, large: `LETTERS THAT LAST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember a letter you kept. Settle, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind one message someone sent you that you never threw away. A birthday card in a drawer. A note from a grandparent. A voicemail you still haven't deleted. A text you saved. Picture it as clearly as you can: the handwriting, the voice, the first line. Ask yourself why you kept it. What did it say that still holds? If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Hukamnama. A letter carrying the Guru's hukam to a sangat, and today also the name for the hymn read when the Guru Granth Sahib is opened each morning. Today's word.
Your line: letters that last. Today, find that kept letter and read it again, slowly. Then send someone a few lines worth keeping. Day eight hundred thirty-five.

836.title: The people close
836.hook: the story was never only ten men; it was a whole sangat
836.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the family, companions and friends of the Gurus in kirtan, in katha and in the stories told at gurdwaras, and the sangat, the gathered community, is central to Sikh worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hukamnama, the Guru's letter to a far-off sangat, read aloud and kept. Your line was letters that last. Did your letter go out? Today, the last day of this stretch of the path, and a look at everyone in it. Day eight hundred thirty-six.

A painting of a Guru's court. The Guru sits at the center, under a canopy, and that's where the eye goes first. But stay with it a moment longer. At the edges are other figures. Someone waving the chaur. A musician with an instrument. A woman at the side. A man carrying water. An old man with a white beard. A visitor in a Sufi's cap. Each figure was painted by someone who thought they belonged in the picture. The center only makes sense because of the edges. Today: the people close.
screen: `A PAINTING OF THE COURT.` → `THE EYE GOES TO THE CENTER.` → `THE EDGES ARE FULL OF PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: For the last stretch of days, we've been looking at the edges of the painting. Start with family. Mata Tripta and Mehta Kalu, with their love and worry. Bebe Nanaki, the sister who stood by her brother. Mata Sulakhni, steady at home. Mata Khivi, with her generous kitchen. Bibi Amro, whose song changed a life. Bibi Bhani, who held the stool steady. Mata Ganga, Mata Nanaki, Bibi Viro, Mata Gujri. Mata Jito, Mata Sundari, Mata Sahib Kaur. Then the servants and companions. Baba Buddha, who served Guru after Guru. Bhai Gurdas, who was tested too. Bhai Bidhi Chand, a thief turned true. Kirpa Ram, who came back to serve. Daya Singh and the rest of the five, the Panj Pyare. Sangat Singh, who took the Guru's place. Moti Ram Mehra with warm milk. Mai Bhago, who led them back. Bhai Mani Singh, the steady scribe. Bhai Jaita, called the Guru's own son. And the friends: Mian Mir, Budhu Shah, Nabi Khan and Ghani Khan, the Nawab of Malerkotla, Todar Mal, Rai Kalha. And the far-off sangats waiting for letters. Gurbani has a word for this. Sangat, the company, and sat sangat, the true company. Guru Nanak asks, on Ang 72, how the true company is known, and answers: it's where the one Name is praised. That's a paraphrase. In other words, the Gurus' story was never ten men alone on a stage. It was a gathering, and the gathering is part of the teaching. Next, the path turns to a hard stretch for the Khalsa, and it begins at Nanded, with an ascetic who will become a servant.
screen: `FAMILY AT THE EDGES.` · `SERVANTS AND COMPANIONS.` · `FRIENDS OF EVERY FAITH.` · `THE TRUE COMPANY.` · then, large: `A WHOLE SANGAT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name your sangat. Settle, and let the breath slow. Picture your own life as a painting, with you somewhere near the middle. Now look to the edges. Who's there? Name them, one at a time, silently. Family who worried for you. Friends who stood close. Someone of another faith who opened a door. Someone far away who still writes. Someone who did a quiet job you rarely noticed. Let each name have one breath. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
sat sangat, the true company. Guru Nanak says on Ang 72 that it's where the one Name is praised; the family, servants, companions and friends around the Gurus are part of it. Today's word.
Your line: a whole sangat. Today, write down the names from your sit, and tell one of them they're part of yours. Day eight hundred thirty-six.

837.title: Madho Das the ascetic
837.hook: at Nanded the Guru meets a Bairagi ascetic who becomes Banda, the servant
837.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the meeting of Guru Gobind Singh and Madho Das at Nanded as the beginning of Banda Singh Bahadur's story, and remember that he first named himself the Guru's banda, his servant.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed a long stretch on the people around the Gurus. Your line was a whole sangat. Who did you name as yours? Today a new block begins, and it opens far from Punjab. Day eight hundred thirty-seven.

A hermitage by a river at Nanded, deep in the south. Its master is away. His disciples keep the place the way he likes it, and one thing above all: nobody sits on his cot. Then a traveler arrives with his Sikhs, walks in, and sits down on it as if he lives there. The disciples are horrified. Tradition says they try everything they know to tip the stranger off that cot, and nothing moves him. Someone runs to fetch the master. The traveler is Guru Gobind Singh. The master hurrying home is an ascetic named Madho Das.
screen: `A HERMITAGE AT NANDED.` → `NOBODY SITS ON THE MASTER'S COT.` → `A STRANGER SITS DOWN.`

segments.voice: Madho Das was a Bairagi, a renunciant, someone who had let go of attachment. He had left home and family behind, lived as a holy man, and gathered his own followers. Tradition says people feared his powers. So picture him arriving, out of breath, at his own door, and finding a man calmly sitting where no one is allowed to sit. Sikh tellings vary in the details, but the heart of the meeting is a short exchange. Madho Das asks who this is. The Guru answers, in effect, that it's someone Madho Das already knows. And something in Madho Das gives way. He says he is the Guru's banda. The word means servant, even bondsman. Not a title anyone would choose to make himself look important. That's the turn the Sikh story cares about. Here was a man who had already given up the world, and the Guru's call was not to give up more, but to come back into it: to carry a household's burdens, a people's troubles, and to serve. In the Sikh telling, the hermit's discipline isn't thrown away. It gets a new direction. Tradition says he takes amrit and becomes Banda Singh, though tellings differ on the name he received. Sikhs also remember him as Bahadur, the brave. But the name that stuck first is the one he gave himself at the cot. The servant. The next stretch of this path, the Khalsa's hard years, begins with him, and some of it is difficult to hear. It's worth noticing that it doesn't begin with a battle. It begins with one man deciding whom he serves.
screen: `A BAIRAGI WHO LET GO OF THE WORLD.` · `HE FINDS THE GURU ON HIS COT.` · `I AM YOUR BANDA.` · `CALLED BACK INTO THE WORLD TO SERVE.` · then, large: `THE SERVANT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: become someone's servant, quietly, for one task. Sit comfortably and let the breath slow. Notice where you usually sit in your own day: the seat nobody else takes, the routine nobody interrupts. Then think of one person whose day would be lighter if you set that seat aside for a while. A parent, a neighbor, a coworker, a friend. Choose one plain task you could do for them, and picture yourself doing it without being asked and without mentioning it afterward. Hold that picture through the sit. If you pray, you can repeat Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Madho Das. The Bairagi holy man at Nanded who, in Sikh tradition, met Guru Gobind Singh, called himself the Guru's banda, and became Banda Singh. Today's word.
Your line: the servant. Today, do the one task you chose in the sit, for the person you chose, and let nobody thank you for it if you can help it. Day eight hundred thirty-seven.

838.title: Five arrows north
838.hook: tradition says the Guru sent Banda north with five arrows and five Sikhs
838.howItsDone: Sikhs tell how Guru Gobind Singh sent Banda Singh to Punjab with five arrows, five Sikhs and letters to the sangats, and remember the instructions tradition says came with them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hermit at Nanded called himself the Guru's banda. Your line was the servant. Whose task did you quietly take on? Today the servant is sent somewhere. Day eight hundred thirty-eight.

Five arrows. Not a sword, not a crown, not a treasury. Tradition says that when Guru Gobind Singh sent Banda Singh away from Nanded, toward a Punjab he barely knew, those arrows from the Guru's own quiver were among the things he carried. With them came five Sikhs to ride beside him, a drum and a banner, and letters from the Guru telling the Sikhs of Punjab to stand with this man. A long road north, and a stranger at the front of it. Today: five arrows north.
screen: `FIVE ARROWS FROM THE GURU'S QUIVER.` → `FIVE SIKHS, A DRUM, A BANNER.` → `A LONG ROAD NORTH.`

segments.voice: Why would anyone hand a man arrows instead of an army? Sikh tradition reads them as something closer to a seal than a weapon. Five arrows can't win a war. What they could do was say, to anyone who saw them, the Guru sent me. In Punjab, Banda Singh was unknown. He had spent his life as a holy man in other places. The Sikhs there had every reason to ask who he was and why they should follow him. So he carried signs they would recognize: the arrows, the companions, and the Guru's letters. Then there's the number. Five keeps turning up in the Sikh story. Five beloved ones stood up at the first amrit. Five Sikhs ride north here. Tradition doesn't explain every five, and it doesn't need to. Some readers take the pattern to say this mission belongs to the Khalsa, not to one man. That fits what the Sikh tellings say came with the arrows: instructions. Tradition says the Guru told Banda Singh to keep to truth and a disciplined life, to never set himself up as a Guru, and to remember that he served the Khalsa. In other words, the arrows came with a limit attached. Authority was given, and a limit was given in the same breath. Some readers find in this a habit worth keeping. When you're trusted with a task, you're trusted with two things: the job, and the reminder of whose job it really is. Banda Singh set out with both. Tomorrow, the road reaches a hard town.
screen: `ARROWS AS A SEAL, NOT A WEAPON.` · `A STRANGER NEEDS SIGNS.` · `FIVE: THE MISSION BELONGS TO THE KHALSA.` · `AUTHORITY GIVEN WITH A LIMIT.` · then, large: `FIVE ARROWS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: set out on one task. Sit, and let the breath settle into its own pace. Bring to mind something you've been sent to do, by someone else or by your own conscience, that you keep not starting. Name it in a few plain words. Then ask two questions, slowly. First, who trusted me with this? Second, what's the limit, the thing I mustn't do while I do it? Hold both answers through the sit, like a few arrows in your hand. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
teer, an arrow. One of the five from Guru Gobind Singh's own quiver that, tradition says, Banda Singh carried north to Punjab, with five Sikhs, as a sign the Guru had sent him. Today's word.
Your line: five arrows. Today, take the first real step on the task you named in the sit, and keep its limit in mind while you do. Day eight hundred thirty-eight.

839.title: Samana, 1709
839.hook: Banda's growing army takes Samana, home of those who executed Guru Tegh Bahadur
839.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Samana as an early town taken in Banda Singh Bahadur's campaign, and often discuss it alongside the Gurus' teaching that force may be used only against oppression and never from hatred.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Banda Singh rode north carrying the Guru's arrows and the Guru's limits. Your line was five arrows. Did you take the first step on your task? Today the road reaches a town. Day eight hundred thirty-nine.

Here's a question with no comfortable answer. If someone had killed a person you loved, and years later you had the power to reach them, what would you call what you did next? In Punjab, people began to gather around Banda Singh: farmers, villagers, Sikhs who had read the Guru's letters. His following grew into an army. And the town it struck early on was Samana. Tradition says Samana was home to the men who had carried out the execution of Guru Tegh Bahadur. Today: Samana.
screen: `WHAT WOULD YOU CALL IT?` → `A FOLLOWING BECOMES AN ARMY.` → `THE TOWN IS SAMANA.`

segments.voice: Sikh tellings remember Samana as the place where Banda Singh's campaign began to answer the wrongs done to the Gurus. The town was taken by force. Accounts of that day are harsh, and they don't agree on every detail. That honesty belongs in the story; a path that remembers its own martyrs carefully should remember a fallen town carefully too. So what does the carry mean, justice, not revenge? Start with the opening lines of the Guru Granth Sahib. Those words, the Mul Mantar, describe the One as nirbhau and nirvair: without fear, and without enmity. Japji, a morning prayer, begins with them. No hatred lives in the One they turn toward. That sets a hard standard for anyone who picks up a sword in the Guru's name. Here is one way to hear the difference. Revenge looks backward and spreads. It wants the other side to hurt the way you hurt, and it rarely knows when to stop. Justice looks at a specific wrong, aims at the ones responsible, and is meant to end. Sikh tellings hold that the sword is lifted only to stop oppression, not to feed a grudge. Some readers hold Banda Singh's campaign up to that standard and honor it. Others ask hard questions about what happened to ordinary people in the towns that fell. Both are part of how this story is told. What doesn't change is the line the Mul Mantar draws: whatever you do, you are not meant to do it from hatred.
screen: `SAMANA IS TAKEN BY FORCE.` · `ACCOUNTS ARE HARSH, AND DIFFER.` · `NIRBHAU, NIRVAIR: NO FEAR, NO ENMITY.` · `REVENGE SPREADS. JUSTICE ENDS.` · then, large: `JUSTICE, NOT REVENGE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: reflect on justice without revenge. Sit, and let your shoulders drop. Bring to mind a wrong that was done to you or to someone you love. Not the worst one. One you can hold for two minutes. Ask, quietly: what would make this right? Then ask: what would only make them hurt? Notice that the two answers aren't the same, and notice which one your body leans toward. You don't have to settle anything. Just let the difference become clear. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Samana. A town in Punjab that, tradition says, was home to the executioners of Guru Tegh Bahadur, and that Banda Singh's army took by force. Today's word.
Your line: justice, not revenge. Today, when something feels unfair, ask what would make it right, and leave the rest alone. Day eight hundred thirty-nine.

840.title: Chappar Chiri, 1710
840.hook: at Chappar Chiri Banda's forces defeat Wazir Khan, the governor who ordered the Sahibzade's deaths
840.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the battle of Chappar Chiri and the taking of Sirhind as the end of Wazir Khan, who ordered the deaths of the younger Sahibzade, and greet one another with the words that the victory belongs to Waheguru.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Samana, and a hard line between two things that look alike. Your line was justice, not revenge. When something felt unfair, what would have made it right? Today the week ends on a field. Day eight hundred forty.

Go back, for a moment, to a cold tower in Sirhind. Earlier on this path you sat with Mata Gujri and the Guru's two youngest sons, Zorawar Singh and Fateh Singh, held there in the winter, and with the order that ended the boys' lives. The man who gave that order was the governor of Sirhind, Wazir Khan. Sikh memory kept that name. Now the story arrives at a stretch of open ground outside Sirhind called Chappar Chiri, where Banda Singh's army and Wazir Khan's forces meet. Today: Chappar Chiri.
screen: `A COLD TOWER IN SIRHIND.` → `THE GOVERNOR WHO GAVE THE ORDER.` → `AN OPEN FIELD: CHAPPAR CHIRI.`

segments.voice: Sikh tellings describe a hard fight on that field. Tradition remembers Banda Singh's army as farmers and villagers as much as soldiers, facing a well-armed governor's force. By the end of the day, tradition says, Wazir Khan had fallen, and Sirhind itself was taken after. So the carry is two plain words: it came. The answer to that winter order finally came. But listen to what Sikhs say when they greet each other. Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki Fateh. The Khalsa belongs to Waheguru, and so does the victory. Fateh means victory, and here's a detail worth holding: it's also the name of the youngest of those two boys in the tower. Fateh Singh. The victory on the field doesn't belong to Banda Singh, in the Sikh way of saying it. It belongs to Waheguru. And it doesn't give anything back. No battle gives back two boys, or the grandmother who died beside them. That's why the carry is only it came, and not we won. An ending arrived. It closed one long wait. It didn't erase what was lost. This also closes a week. It began with far-off sangats, the letters that kept them close, and a last look at the people around the Gurus. Then a hermit at Nanded became a servant, carried five arrows north, and faced the question of justice at Samana. Today the long wait for Sirhind reaches its end.
screen: `A HARD FIGHT ON AN OPEN FIELD.` · `WAZIR KHAN FALLS; SIRHIND IS TAKEN.` · `THE VICTORY BELONGS TO WAHEGURU.` · `AN ENDING DOESN'T GIVE BACK THE LOST.` · then, large: `IT CAME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with a long-awaited ending. Settle, and breathe slowly. Think of something you waited a long time for: a diagnosis, an apology, a verdict, a door closing, a letter. Remember the moment it finally came. Notice what it gave you, and notice honestly what it couldn't give back. Let both sit side by side without choosing between them. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out, and let the ending belong to something bigger than you. The bell holds the time.
Chappar Chiri. The field near Sirhind where, in Sikh tradition, Banda Singh's army met the forces of Wazir Khan, who fell there. Today's word.
Your line: it came. Today, think of one person still waiting for an ending, and send them a word that says you haven't forgotten. Day eight hundred forty.
